title: A comparative study of the Indonesia-Malaysia border regions
abstract: This study aims to investigate the socio-cultural, economic, and educational aspects of border communities between Indonesia and Malaysia, with a focus on the Malay and Dayak ethnic groups in Paloh (Sambas Regency) and Jagoi Babang (Bengkayang Regency). Persistent disparities in welfare, educational quality, and national integration in Indonesia’s border regions have weakened nationalism and increased socio-economic dependence on Malaysia. On the border, civic education plays a crucial role in strengthening Indonesian nationalism, despite the community’s economic dependence on Malaysia. Through flag ceremonies, character education, and the integration of local wisdom into the curriculum, schools function as the final bastion of nationalism, safeguarding the national identity of the younger generation in the face of economic inequality and transnational influences. Using a qualitative approach that integrates ethnographic and etnopedagogic methods, data were collected through participatory observation, semi-structured interviews, and document analysis. The findings indicate that Indonesian border communities experience a dual identity, marked by both symbolic loyalty to Indonesia an

title: Implementation and violations of election principles in the 2024 Presidential and Vice-Presidential elections of the Republic of Indonesia
abstract: This study examines the implementation of electoral principles mandated in Article 22E of the 1945 Constitution—direct, universal, free, confidential, honest, and fair elections—in the 2024 Indonesian presidential and vice-presidential elections, which were marked by legal controversy following Constitutional Court Decision Number 90/PUU-XXI/2023. A socio-legal approach was employed, combining document analysis, in-depth interviews, and focus group discussions with election organisers and supervisory bodies. Data were analysed qualitatively using the Miles, Huberman, and Saldana interactive model, involving data reduction, display, and conclusion drawing. The principles of direct and universal suffrage were generally upheld. However, the principles of free, confidential, honest, and fair elections were only partially implemented. Violations identified include money politics, lack of institutional neutrality, power intervention, and vote mobilisation practices. These findings indicate persistent structural weaknesses in Indonesia’s electoral democracy, particularly in the 2024 elections. Roots and resilience: Tracing the rise of conservative Islamic movements in Indonesia
abstract: Although Indonesia is not formally an Islamic state, the idea of establishing one has remained a recurring theme in the country’s political discourse. From the pre-independence period to the reform era, discussions surrounding the Islamic state have persisted and never entirely disappeared. The notion continues to develop, reflecting the aspirations of specific segments of Indonesia's Muslim population. These groups, often referred to as conservative Islamic factions, are characterised by their adherence to textual interpretations of Islamic teachings and their desire to integrate religion and state within a legal and governmental framework. The emergence of conservative Islamic groups in Indonesia was not a spontaneous phenomenon. Instead, their development follows a long historical trajectory traceable to the pre-independence or nationalist movement period, when the country was still under colonial rule. During this era, the embryonic idea of an Islamic state began to take shape within Sarekat Islam (SI), the most prominent Islamic organisation in the archipelago. A The Indonesia-Malaysia border as a simulacrum of nationalism: A hyperreality study of the Jagoi Babang community in West Kalimantan
abstract: In this article, we investigate how the simulacra perpetrated by Malaysia and the efforts of the border communities of Jagoi Babang to maintain their identity through a spirit of nationalism towards Indonesia. The border region is a complex space that requires a thorough understanding to avoid being affected by the simulacra perpetrated by the neighbouring country. Drawing on Baudrillard's theories of hyperreality and simulacra, this research explores how border communities filter the various simulacra efforts by Malaysia to change the reality of border communities towards Indonesia. A case study approach involving observation, documentation, and interviews with 15 informants from various backgrounds. The research findings show that the Malaysian state performs simulacra by providing easy access to various facilities, such as educational and health services, as well as to economic opportunities, such as shopping and the use of the ringgit in transactions. In addition, this study shows the efforts of border communities to filter simulacra by strengthening nationalism in Indonesia through the use of Indonesian and local languages, as well as through cultural defence, regularly conduc

title: Digital citizenship for sustainable development goals: A character-based approach in civic education
Collective resistance and institutional change: Feminist movements and victims' organizations in Mexico’s fight against impunity
abstract: Mexico faces a crisis of impunity marked by femicidal violence, disappearances, and institutional flaws. This study examines how feminist and victims' groups resist impunity by analysing their strategies, conditions for change, and justice reforms. Using mixed methods, the research analysed 847 events from 2014-2024 through content analysis, along with 32 interviews and 385 documents. Techniques like regression and network analysis identified patterns and key factors. Movements fight impunity by exposing state failures, creating alternative knowledge, using international frameworks, disrupting normalcy, and raising visibility. title: Social media: A means of developing generation z's political participation in the digital era
abstract: This article elaborates on generation Z's information seeking patterns through social media and the development of their political participation. This research used a qualitative - descriptive design, conducted in the city of Pekanbaru with 296 generation Z who were interviewed directly and by filling in a Google form. The research was conducted in the time span of September-October 2024. Data analysis techniques used the Miles and Huberman model. The triangulation technique uses data source triangulation. The research results found that (1) 69.9% of informants preferred to use social media in searching for political information compared to news websites (24.7%), television (1%) and YouTube channels (1%) for the reasons that they were easy to access and understand, practical , more complete and up to date, as well as a more attractive appearance and does not contain much writing; (2) 57.1% of informants follow certain politicians' accounts and 42.9% say they do not follow them. Regarding political news posts on social media, 33% of informants stated that they often left comments on these posts and others did not. Mapping the “Aksi Bela Islam 212” effect: Redefining identity politics in Indonesian scholarship 2011–2023
abstract: Although identity politics dominates contemporary debates, little systematic research has examined how its discursive use has narrowed interpretations in Indonesia. This study addresses that gap by tracing shifts in Indonesian academic discourse between 2011 and 2023 through a systematic literature review and content analysis of sixty peer-reviewed articles, using Foucault’s genealogical approach. The findings show that during the baseline period of 2011–2015, identity politics was framed mainly as a cultural and ethnic phenomenon or as the logical consequence of plural democracy. A major rupture occurred in 2016–2017, coinciding with the “Aksi Bela Islam 212” movement and the Jakarta gubernatorial election, when religious identity was electorally mobilised and quickly institutionalised as the dominant academic frame. By 2019, academic discourse overwhelmingly reduced identity politics to a nexus between religion and elections, often framed in terms of polarisation and threats to democracy. Meanwhile, alternative articulations such as gender or ethnic empowerment appeared only sporadically and remained marginalised. This narrowing indicates how Indonesian scholarship has privileged

title: Project citizen digital: A learning model of civic education in digital age
Assessing student readiness through artificial intelligence-based comics to enhance literacy and Indonesian local wisdom values
abstract: This study aimed to measure students’ readiness to implement artificial intelligence-based project learning by strengthening local wisdom values in Indonesia. Using a quantitative survey method, the participants in this study were 285 program students from universities in Indonesia, namely Universitas Muhammadiyah Ponorogo, Universitas Muhammadiyah Makassar, Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia, and Universitas Negeri Yogyakarta, who were randomly assigned to ensure balanced representation across academic years. The study was an online, objective test on an artificial intelligence-based project aimed at strengthening local wisdom values. Data analysis was used with descriptive quantitative methods. The results of the analysis showed that students’ readiness in artificial intelligence-based project learning for strengthening local wisdom values was at the “good” level of awareness, while other indicators were at the “fair” and “poor” levels, indicating the need for further improvement on artificial intelligence-based project learning for strengthening local wisdom values in Indonesia. These findings underscore the importance of integrating artificial intelligence-based project learning

title: Democratic regression and the rise of electoral illiberalism in Indonesia: A multi-dimensional analysis (1998-2024)
abstract: Since the political transition of 1998, Indonesia has been widely regarded as a leading case of democratic consolidation in Southeast Asia. However, recent empirical indicators reveal a persistent decline in civil liberties, political pluralism, and institutional accountability. This article examines whether Indonesia is experiencing democratic regression and investigates the emergence of electoral illiberalism as a durable regime trajectory rather than a temporary fluctuation. Methodologically, this study employs qualitative thematic-narrative analysis, triangulating constitutional amendments, electoral laws, Constitutional Court decisions, and executive regulations with international democracy indices, including the Economist Intelligence Unit and Freedom House, from 1998 to 2024. This approach enables a longitudinal assessment of institutional and normative transformations across key democratic dimensions. The findings demonstrate that democratic regression in Indonesia is not marked by the collapse of electoral competition, but by the weakening of horizontal accountability, erosion of the rule of law through systemic corruption, contraction of civic space, and strategic mobiliz

title: Beyond quotas: Women’s substantive participation and democratic consolidation in Timor-Leste
abstract: Women’s participation in public policy-making is a cornerstone of democratic governance, especially in post-conflict contexts such as Timor-Leste. Despite achieving 38% parliamentary representation in 2023 through quota legislation, women’s substantive influence remains constrained by entrenched patriarchal norms, elite gatekeeping, institutional weaknesses, and persistent gender-based violence. This study addresses a critical gap in the literature by shifting the analytical focus from descriptive representation to substantive representation—examining how women shape policy agendas, exercise agency, and contribute to governance outcomes once inside institutions. Employing a systematic literature review (2015–2025) guided by PRISMA 2020, the research synthesises peer-reviewed studies, institutional reports, and policy documents. The analysis is framed through critical actor theory, feminist institutionalism, and intersectionality, highlighting how formal and informal dynamics intersect to shape women’s agency. Findings reveal three dimensions. First, women face structural, institutional, and cultural barriers that limit their influence on policy despite numerical gains. Second, stra

title: Reimagining citizenship in electoral times: Lessons from Gen Z’s digital civics prototypes for Indonesia’s 2024 election
abstract: This study examines how the Indonesian Generation Z reimagines the role of citizenship in electoral democracy by developing 11 digital civic prototypes for the 2024 election. This study used Schreier's Qualitative Content Analysis method on prototype documents developed by students of the Political Science Study Program at Brawijaya University. The analysis maps three dimensions of Marshallian rights civil, political, and social and the Westheimer-Kahne citizen typology, adding the categories of digital acts and connective action. The results showed a paradigm shift in citizenship from passive voters to participatory citizens through transparent access to candidate information, online channels for public aspirations, and discussion forums for political deliberation. The majority of prototypes emphasize digital-political literacy and the inclusion of young, first-time, and out-of-town voters by utilizing simple language, infographics, and interactive social media campaigns, including elements of gamification and peer mobilization typical of Gen Z. Dimensions of democratic ethics such as anti-abstention education and anti-money politics are quite strong, but social justice orientatio

title: Mapping of global citizenship research in Indonesia 2011-2025: A bibliometric study
abstract: This study explores the landscape of global citizenship education (GCE) in Indonesia from 2011 to 2025. Despite being a critical issue closely linked to national values such as Pancasila and religious moderation, the current discourse remains fragmented. Using a bibliometric approach with the Bibliometrix R package and Scopus data, the research maps publication trends, keywords, and collaboration networks. Findings reveal a significant surge in publications since 2019, peaking in 2023, driven by Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and national policy shifts. While character education and democracy remain dominant themes, newer topics like digital citizenship and religious moderation are emerging. However, research is heavily concentrated in Javanese teacher-training institutions and lacks global collaboration. Vital gaps include a low integration of ecological issues and a limited interdisciplinary focus. The study concludes that future research must bridge these gaps by prioritising digital literacy and environmental sustainability within the framework of Indonesian citizenship education

title: Institutional isomorphism and community politicisation: A theoretical and empirical comparison between Indonesia and Japan
abstract: This research aims to explore how global pressures, international standards, and institutional structures affect the development and effectiveness of community politicisation, focusing on the similarities and differences between the two countries. This research uses a qualitative method, analysing secondary data from interviews, digital platforms, and public sources, complemented by textual analysis and social network analysis. These findings highlight the key role of isomorphism in standardising politicisation practices, with Indonesia and Japan both adopting community politicisation models to increase public trust and cooperation. However, significant differences were observed in the execution of these models, especially in the level of community involvement and the historical context of their implementation. While Japan's political system has matured through policies and structures such as "koban" and "chuzaisyo", Indonesia faces challenges related to limited resources and community diversity. The research concludes that the success of community politicisation depends on the effective adaptation of isomorphisms to local needs, emphasising the importance of community participatio

title: Navigating citizenship in an era of global uncertainty
Police transformation within constitutional democracy design: Evidence from Indonesia
abstract: Polri's institutional position following the 1998 political transition remains a contested terrain, particularly in reconciling operational independence with the demands of democratic governance. This study investigates how Polri has navigated that tension, drawing on a mixed-methods design that integrates diagnostic mapping of 130 institutional problems, structured surveys with 167 experts distributed across 50 districts and cities, and comparative analysis of policing frameworks in France and the Netherlands. The findings expose a fundamental contradiction within Act No. 2/2002: while the legislation formally separates Polri from military structures, it simultaneously creates an accountability vacuum, a concern reflected in the 61.7% unfavorable expert assessments. Field data further document three entrenched dysfunctions a militaristic organizational culture, integrity failures concentrated in investigative units, and chronic service deficiencies flagged repeatedly in ombudsman evaluations between 2020 and 2023. Building on these findings, the study advances a transformation framework organized around four mutually reinforcing pillars: humanist policing grounded in rights protec

title: AI-driven service quality and customer engagement: The mediating role of digital empathy and cognitive absorption
abstract: The aim of this study is to investigate how AI-driven service quality (AISQ) influences customer engagement (CE) in the e-commerce industry in Pakistan. This study examines the mediation of digital empathy (DE) and cognitive absorption (CA). It concerns discovering how AI-driven service quality affects customer interactions through emotional and cognitive processes. Through an online survey, data were collected from 321 e-commerce clients in Pakistan. The current study used convenience sampling. A five-point questionnaire was used for data collection. The statistical tool SPSS 22.0 was used for correlation and regression analysis. The conceptual framework was built on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Trust-Commitment Theory (TCT) to determine the association among AISQ, DE, CA, and CE. The proposed hypotheses and their mediation effects were tested using Structural Equation Modelling (SEM). The findings of the present study indicate that AISQ has a positive impact on CE. DE and CA play an important role in mediating this relationship. The results of this study show that when customers perceive AI-based services as empathetic and interesting, they are more likely to bec

title: The influence of teachers’ professional and pedagogical competence on the enhancement of students’ civic knowledge
Validity test of digital learning content in social science education for junior high schools in Singaraja city
abstract: This study seeks to examine the requirements for creating digital learning resources in Social Sciences education at junior high schools in Singaraja City. This research employed qualitative methodologies. The development of learning media must involve testing for construct validity and empirical validity. Validity testing will be conducted by specialists in materials, media, and language. The evaluation conducted by experts in Social Sciences Education determined the validity score of the material to be 93, categorising it as "very valid." Similarly, the graphic design value is rated at 90, categorising it as "Very Valid." Simultaneously, the degree of grammatical validity is 88, categorised as "Very Valid." The expert testing results in media, material, and language aspects indicate that the developed digital learning media is highly valid and thus appropriate for the Social Sciences Education learning process. The practicality of digital learning media was evaluated by two groups from Social Science Education and 24 students participating in Social Science Education instruction. The mean score awarded by Social Sciences Education instructors was 87.69, categorised as Very Good.

title: Strengthening digital literacy and political culture for gen-Z through Pancasila education learning in higher education
abstract: This article reviews the importance of political culture and digital literacy for Generation Z as a prospective demographic group. It examines how Pancasila education contributes to the development of Gen-Z's political culture and literacy in higher education. Using a mixed-method research approach with a sequential transformative strategy model, the study transforms one type of data into another after collecting and analyzing quantitative and qualitative data independently. Research findings indicate that trending topics, viral hashtags, FYP, news feeds, CC, and social media algorithms form the foundation of Gen-Z's digital political literacy and culture. This illustrates that, despite avoiding direct practice, Gen-Z exhibits a keen interest in digital politics. Consequently, Pancasila education provides Gen-Z members with opportunities to become competent political players and participants. The study also shows how Pancasila education incorporates digital-based political literacy and culture by emphasizing civic duties and integrating more "real" materials and ideals. The findings suggest that Pancasila education can enhance Gen-Z's digital political literacy and culture by makin

title: Legal compliance in market retribution payments
abstract: The objective of this study is to critically examine traders' legal compliance practices concerning the payment of market retribution. Additionally, it aims to investigate the factors that impact the policies and efforts made by market managers. This study employs a qualitative research method, utilizing a case study approach that includes observation, interviews, and documentation as components of the research process. The study's findings demonstrate that vendors' compliance with the law regarding the payment of market fees continues to be minimal. The factors that impact the implementation of these policies include perceptions among vendors that they personally own their stalls, poor-quality market services, unstable economic conditions among vendors, and insufficient supervision and enforcement of penalties. Efforts made by market managers to improve traders' compliance are still limited to socialisation and manual collection, without the assistance of a system that is both effective and transparent. According to these findings, there is not only a connection between legal compliance in fee payments and individual legal awareness, but perceptions of fairness, legitimacy, and pa

title: Civic engagement of Tengger indigenous community in strengthening ecological citizenship
abstract: This study aims to analyze the involvement of the Tengger Indigenous People in strengthening ecological citizenship. Using a case study approach, this research examines how the values of Tri Hita Karana which emphasize harmony between humans and God (parahyangan), among fellow humans (pawongan), and with the environment (palemahan) support sustainable nature conservation practices. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, participatory observation, and documentation involving traditional leaders, community members, and key stakeholders in the Tengger region. The findings reveal that civic engagement rooted in local wisdom contributes to the preservation of natural resources such as water, reduces soil erosion, and promotes the sustainability of the Mount Bromo ecosystem. Moreover, collective community participation through traditional rituals such as Kasada and Entas-entas serves as a mechanism for fostering environmental awareness and strengthening social cohesion. These findings align with the theory of ecological citizenship, which posits that local community involvement in environmental stewardship is a critical factor in ensuring ecological sustainability. title: The ebb and flow of the relationship between the institutional and authority of the directorate general of immigration and the directorate of general legal administration
abstract: Since the beginning of independence, the authority to handle citizenship in Indonesia has experienced dynamics closely related to the scope of duties and functions of immigration. This study analyses the institutional relationship and authority between the Directorate General of Immigration and the Directorate General of AHU in handling citizenship in Indonesia. The research method used in this article is normative legal research, or doctrinal legal research. Interview techniques support the exploration of thoughts, views, and opinions related to the research topic. The results of the study indicate that the authority to handle citizenship is always closely related to the duties and functions of immigration, so that the roles of the Directorate General of General Legal Administration (Ditjen AHU) and the Directorate General of Immigration cannot be separated, even though they are administratively separate. However, the institutional relationship between these two institutions continues to face challenges, including weak coordination, overlapping authority, and inefficiencies exacerbated by their placement under different ministries. These issues have led to low operational effectiv

title: Family-based traditional market management in Yogyakarta Special Province Indonesia
abstract: This research aims to examine the implementation of family-based principles in the traditional market management in Yogyakarta. This research is qualitative research employing a case study approach. Data collection methods were interviews and questionnaires. The research subjects consisted of Traditional Market Traders, Market Heads, and five Indonesian Association of Market Traders including Beringharjo, Sleman, Piyungan, Wates, and Wonosari Market. The results of this research show that the family-based principles are applied in the management of these traditional markets. Based on the interview results and questionnaires, traditional market traders, market heads, and traders’ associations have a strong relationship both structurally and formally as well as culturally and informally. Communication between the three research subjects was established effectively by performing deliberations in policy making. Informal relationships include recitals, joint gymnastics, and cooperation. title: The role of community-based schools in enhancing access to quality education in rural Nigeria and South Africa
abstract: This study investigates the role of community-based schools in enhancing access to quality education in rural Nigeria and South Africa. A descriptive survey research design was adopted for the study. The population comprised individuals actively involved with community-based schools in selected rural communities across both countries. A total sample of 300 respondents (150 from Nigeria and 150 from South Africa) was selected using a multi-stage sampling technique involving purposive, stratified, and simple random sampling methods. Data were collected using a structured instrument titled Community-Based Schools Educational Access and Quality Questionnaire (CBSEAQ). The instrument’s validity was established through expert review for content and face validity, while its reliability was confirmed through a pilot test, yielding a Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.82. Trained research assistants administered the questionnaire and ensured informed consent and respondent anonymity. The researchers analysed the data using SPSS, employing descriptive statistics and inferential tests such as t-tests and chi-square tests to compare responses between countries. The findings revealed that commun

title: The differential effects of critical thinking and digital literacy on civic engagement in project-based civic learning: Evidence from Indonesian higher education
abstract: This study examined how critical thinking and digital literacy contribute to civic engagement among pre-service primary school teachers in a Civic Education course using Project-Based Civic Learning (PjBCL) at an Indonesian university. Using a quantitative correlational design, data from 126 students were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling. Pre-post gains were large for critical thinking (d = 1.116), digital literacy (d = 1.418) and civic engagement (d = 1.726). The two competencies operated through different mechanisms. Critical thinking partially mediated the effect of PjBCL on civic engagement (indirect effect = 0.038; 95% CI [0.012, 0.072]), whereas digital literacy did not. Although digital literacy was the strongest direct predictor of civic engagement (β = 0.350; f² = 0.124), its link with PjBCL was negligible (β = 0.004; Q² = 0.001), suggesting students develop it mainly through informal online engagement rather than the curriculum. Building on dual-process theory, the study proposes Digitally Scaffolded Civic Learning (DSCL), which embeds digital literacy in each stage of project-based civic instruction, offering implications for curriculum p

title: Economic behaviour as a form of citizenship: Evidence from the Dayak, Malay, and Chinese communities in Sekadau District
abstract: This study examines how cultural values shape economic behaviour as a practice of citizenship among the Dayak, Malay and Chinese communities of Sekadau Regency, West Kalimantan, Indonesia. Moving beyond reductionist and market-centred approaches, it treats economic activity not merely as rational financial action but as an expression of values, social responsibilities and civic commitments. Using a qualitative ethnographic-phenomenological design, data were gathered through in-depth interviews with 42 informants, ten months of field observation and document analysis. The findings show that local values, customary norms and social ethics guide economic behaviour in all three communities, producing a typology of cultural citizenship. The Dayak community practises communal citizenship grounded in customary solidarity and harmony with nature. The Malay community enacts ethical citizenship, integrating Islamic values, honesty and contentment into market conduct. The Chinese community demonstrates productive citizenship through disciplined family enterprise, trust-based networks and mutual assistance. Despite these differences, all three patterns foster civic consciousness, social partic

title: Beyond consensus: Negotiating climate citizenship through deliberative communication in school-based climate action
abstract: This study critically examines deliberative democracy within school-based climate action, contending that student agency and participation in climate citizenship education are shaped by communicative processes rather than solely by individual capability. While environmental education increasingly addresses climate change, instrumental and technocratic approaches continue to restrict authentic democratic engagement. Employing a critical ethnographic methodology informed by Habermasian communicative action and Freirean critical pedagogy, data were collected from a school-based climate action programme involving teachers, students, and external facilitators. The findings indicate that deliberative processes are shaped by communicative, instrumental, and strategic rationalities, resulting in asymmetrical negotiation, partial compromise, and contingent consensus. Although dialogic spaces foster student participation and critical reflection, these opportunities are constrained by institutional structures, cultural norms, and power relations. The study concludes that student agency is context-dependent and relational, emerging from communicative processes. It recommends repositioning clim

title: Student perceptions of game-based learning in civic education: A Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) approach
abstract: The development of digital technology has brought significant changes to learning practices in higher education, particularly in the use of games that are close to students' lives. This study aims to analyze students' perceptions of game-based learning in civic education using digital game learning media. The study used a quantitative approach, employing a survey, with 120 students from Universitas Negeri Semarang (UNNES) across various study programs and semesters in 2025-2026. The researcher collected data through a Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed it using quantitative descriptive methods within the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), which comprises indicators of perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. The results showed that students had a relatively moderate level of game play and exhibited positive perceptions of the use of digital games as learning media. Students assessed that digital games can increase interest in learning, help understand the material, and have the potential to develop student character traits such as tolerance, appreciation, honesty, and responsibility. However, students also recognized the potential negative impacts, namely the risk of ga

title: Citizenship and the ethics of care: Feminist considerations on justice, morality and politics by Selma Sevenhuijsen
abstract: Citizenship and the Ethics of Care: Feminist Considerations on Justice, Morality and Politics, written by Selma Sevenhuijsen, examines how the ethics of care can enrich contemporary understandings of democracy, citizenship, and public policy. The book critiques the limits of liberal political theory, which rests on the assumption of rational, autonomous individuals and therefore struggles to explain the interdependence of human relationships. Sevenhuijsen does not reject liberalism. She positions care as a normative dimension that complements justice and broadens its meaning, so that justice is understood as a moral practice sensitive to social context and human vulnerability. The book also shifts citizenship from a legal status to a relational ethical practice grounded in responsibility and respect for human dignity, while rejecting the essentialist view that care belongs to women by nature. Its practical value emerges in discussions of family law, child custody, health care, and the welfare state, where care serves as a standard for evaluating public policy. The book has limits: it offers little guidance on institutional implementation, and its empirical illustrations come mostly

title: Deep learning-oriented problem-based learning to foster critical thinking in civic education in primary schools
abstract: How can civic education move beyond transmitting knowledge to cultivating the critical thinking young citizens need for democratic life? This study addresses that question by examining a deep learning-oriented problem-based learning (DL-PBL) model designed to develop critical thinking and support civic learning within primary Civic Education. Using a convergent mixed-methods design, we worked with 112 fourth-grade students from two primary schools in Palembang, South Sumatra, employing a quasi-experimental pre-test–post-test design with intact classes, complemented by classroom observations and students’ reflective journals. Because the total-score distribution was non-normal, between-group differences were analysed using an independent-samples Mann–Whitney U test, which indicated a statistically significant difference in total critical-thinking scores between the two groups, U = 0.000, z = −9.142, p

title: Integrating AI-assisted design thinking in citizenship education: Enhancing university students’ problem analysis and critical thinking skills
abstract: This study aims to analyse the implementation of an AI-assisted design thinking learning model in enhancing university students’ problem analysis and critical thinking skills in Citizenship Education programmes. The study employed a qualitative approach involving undergraduate students from several Citizenship Education programmes at universities on Java Island, Indonesia. The learning implementation integrated artificial intelligence (AI) to assist students in exploring information, generating ideas and reflecting on solutions to civic and social issues. Research data were collected through observations of the learning process, analysis of students’ assignment documents, AI-assisted interaction records and group discussions conducted during the implementation of the model. Data were analysed descriptively to identify the dynamics of the learning process at each stage of design thinking. The findings indicate that AI-assisted design thinking encouraged students to engage actively in social problem analysis and problem-solving. During the empathise stage, students identified social issues through digital information exploration, AI use and group discussions, enabling them to underst

title: Police-led preventive cyber education and cryptocurrency scam prevention: A PRISMA-guided systematic literature review from a digital citizenship perspective
abstract: Cryptocurrency participation has expanded digital economic citizenship while exposing users to fraud that combines technological complexity, social engineering, impersonation, cognitive bias, and irreversible transactions. This systematic literature review examines how police-led preventive cyber education can strengthen protective behaviour against cryptocurrency scams and how this function can be conceptualised within digital citizenship. The review followed PRISMA 2020 reporting principles and PRISMA-S search-documentation elements. A structured cross-platform search and citation-chasing process covered peer-reviewed literature published from January 2015 to 24 August 2026. Forty-seven candidate records were logged, seven duplicates were removed, 40 records were screened, 34 were assessed for full-text relevance, and 30 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Evidence was coded across cybersecurity education and policing, cryptocurrency fraud/literacy/risk, and digital citizenship. The synthesis identifies five persistent gaps: limited direct evidence on police-delivered education for adult crypto users, overreliance on knowledge and intention rather than observed be

title: Digital administrative burden as a civic education problem: A conceptual and methodological framework for digital citizenship, social justice, and citizenship rights among vulnerable groups
abstract: As public services move onto digital platforms, civic education must prepare citizens not only to use technology responsibly but also to understand, claim, and contest the services through which their rights are realised. This article develops a conceptual and methodological framework that reframes digital administrative burden in Indonesia as a problem of citizenship formation and substantive rights. For citizens facing poverty, disability, old age, rural remoteness, or limited literacy, opaque digital procedures do more than create technical difficulty; they erode civic agency. Drawing on administrative burden theory, Marshall's citizenship rights, Sen's capability approach, and digital citizenship scholarship, the article proposes a model linking learning, compliance, and psychological costs to perceived access, service justice, and civic confidence. It situates this model within Indonesian civic education through Pancasila's principle of social justice and outlines a fieldwork protocol for future empirical testing. The article argues that digital access is never merely administrative: it is where citizens learn whether the state recognises them as equal, rights-bearing members

title: Integration of Islamic values in Civic Education learning: A framework for character development in Islamic boarding schools
abstract: Globalisation's pervasive influence has significantly transformed societal norms, particularly affecting students who are vulnerable to value erosion. Quality civic education that integrates religious values is imperative in Islamic boarding school (pesantren) contexts to preserve positive character development. This qualitative case study examines the integration of Islamic values in Civic Education at MTs Azzainiyah, Sukabumi, Indonesia, and proposes a five-dimensional conceptual framework that moves beyond descriptive accounts to reveal operational mechanisms of integration. Through six-month fieldwork involving semi-structured interviews with 24 participants, 24 classroom observations, and analysis of 42 documents, the study identifies five synergistic dimensions: (1) curriculum alignment embedding values in lesson plans and syllabi, (2) pedagogical enactment through differentiated and cooperative learning strategies, (3) textual linking connecting Pancasila principles with Qur'anic verses and hadith, (4) school culture habituation via daily Islamic-civic rituals, and (5) civic virtue projects enabling practical value application through community service. title: Enhancing civic intellectual and participation skills through interactive learning strategies
abstract: Interactive learning strategies are increasingly recognised as central to civic education, yet their contribution to civic intellectual and participation skills remains underexplored. This article examines how interactive learning strategies enhance university students’ civic intellectual and participation skills within an Indonesian higher education setting. Using a qualitative, single instrumental case study design, the study gathered data through participant observation, semi-structured interviews, and documentation involving one lecturer and five students at a state Islamic university in Jakarta, and analysed them using Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña’s interactive data analysis model. The findings show that interactive learning strategies foster active, meaningful, and enjoyable learning by shifting students from passive recipients to active participants, thereby strengthening civic intellectual skills such as critical thinking, analysis, and argumentation, alongside civic participation skills including collaboration, communication, and democratic engagement. Unlike prior studies that emphasise civic knowledge acquisition alone, this article demonstrates that interactive strategi

title: Navigating ‘Ke-Indonesia-an’ in diaspora: Transnational habitus and the construction of national values among migrant children in Sabah, Malaysia, and Semarang, Indonesia
abstract: This study examines the social construction and habituation of Indonesian national identity (ke-Indonesia-an) among early adolescents in two contrasting environments: Semarang, Indonesia, and Sabah, Malaysia. Using a comparative ethnographic design, data were collected through semi-structured interviews, participant observation, and documentary analysis involving 22 participants: 10 students (aged 13–15), 8 parents or guardians, and 4 teachers across three field sites: junior secondary schools in Semarang, Community Learning Centers (CLC) in Sabah, and non-CLC migrant households in Sabah. The analysis integrates Berger and Luckmann's (1966) social constructionism, Bourdieu's (1990) habitus and field theory, and Sayad's (1999) transnational habitus framework. Findings reveal that in Semarang, ke-Indonesia-an is reinforced through coherent institutional mechanisms, producing what Billig (1995) terms “banal nationalism.” In contrast, migrant children in Sabah navigate a fragmented identity process shaped by assimilation pressures, legal precarity, and social stigma, yet sustain “performative nationalism” through CLC education, familial oral histories, and digital media. title: Pancasila, social justice, and the ultimum remedium principle: Reframing criminal tax law as a citizenship issue in Indonesia
abstract: This article reframes the ultimum remedium principle in Indonesian criminal tax law as a problem of fiscal citizenship and Pancasila-based public authority. It asks when criminal enforcement is legitimate, rather than presuming that administrative enforcement is always preferable. The study employs statutory, conceptual, and case approaches. It analyses the 1945 Constitution; Articles 8, 12, 13, 22, 38, 39, 39A, 40, 43A, 44, 44A, 44B, and 44C of the Law on General Provisions and Tax Procedures (KUP Law); and three purposively selected lines of decisions: Supreme Court Decision No. 2239 K/Pid.Sus/2012, Supreme Court Decision No. 1149 K/Pid/2022, and District Court of Boyolali Decision No. 6/Pid.Sus/2023/PN Byl as upheld through Supreme Court Decision No. 4878 K/Pid.Sus/2023. Fiscal citizenship is operationalised through civic trust, civic duty, civic equality, and civic participation, while the Pancasila principles are translated into criteria of integrity, proportionality, legitimacy, accountability, and distributive fairness. The analysis finds that Articles 13 and 40 of KUP Law regulate different legal clocks—administrative assessment and criminal prosecution—and should not be tr

title: Developing a conceptual model for integrating curriculum and eco school activities to strengthen ecological citizenship in boarding schools: A case study of SMAN Titian Teras, Jambi
abstract: Recurring forest and land fires and persistent solid waste mismanagement in Jambi Province point to a gap between environmental knowledge and ecological practice among Indonesian secondary students. This study addresses that gap by developing and testing an Integrated Curriculum and Eco-School Model to strengthen Ecological Citizenship in a boarding school setting. Employing a Research and Development design structured around the ADDIE framework, the study was conducted at SMAN Titian Teras Jambi, a full boarding senior high school. Data were gathered through a student profile questionnaire administered to 120 Year 10 and 11 students, focus group discussions with education experts, and daily behavioural observations in classrooms and dormitories. The resulting model embeds Ecological Citizenship indicators within the learning outcomes of Pancasila Education, Biology, and Economics, and introduces an Eco Block habituation system into dormitory routines, linking instruction to boarding life. Validation by three experts in curriculum design, ecopedagogy, and boarding management produced an average feasibility score of 88.57%. Pre-test and post-test scores, analysed using a paired-samp

title: Rethinking citizenship from Southeast Asia: Recognition, belonging, and unequal rights
abstract: Citizenship scholarship in Southeast Asia examines the uneven relationships between legal membership, social recognition, and access to rights. This editorial argues that the region offers a basis for reconsidering how these relationships are produced across borders, institutions, and generations. Drawing on studies from Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Myanmar, Singapore, and transnational settings, it examines customary belonging, documentary exclusion, and differentiated pathways towards membership. Recognition becomes consequential through the institutions and intermediaries that translate social attachments into enforceable claims, while similar attachments can generate unequal outcomes. The discussion connects these processes to civic education, showing why participation, cultural recognition, and national identification require examination alongside the conditions under which rights become accessible. It proposes a comparative research agenda attentive to administrative encounters, changing biographies, and the distribution of authority within communities. title: Assessing the welfare impact of Yogyakarta’s privilege fund on street vendors affected by the Sultan’s urban order policy
abstract: This study examines the effectiveness of the Special Fund (Danais) in improving community welfare through a case study of street vendor (PKL) relocation in the Malioboro Terrace area and the Abu Bakar Ali Special Parking Area (TKP), Yogyakarta. Using a qualitative descriptive approach, data were collected through in-depth interviews, focus group discussions (FGDs), participatory observation, and policy document analysis, involving stakeholders including street vendors, parking attendants, and local government representatives. The findings reveal that the Danais-financed relocation policy has not delivered meaningful benefits to the affected communities. Key findings include declining revenues, limited participation in planning, and dissatisfaction with new locations and facilities. Although perceptions of social security improved, selling comfort and business sustainability remain significant concerns. These findings suggest that a technocratic approach insufficiently grounded in community needs and participation risks generating new forms of inequality. title: Integrating Krathwohl’s taxonomy into digital self-assessment: Psychometric validation of a civic affective scale for secondary education
abstract: This study develops and evaluates a digital self-assessment tool to measure students' affective domain in Civics Education at the senior high school level. The research addresses the lack of measurement of affective outcomes in civic and character education. Although the affective dimension is an important part of the curriculum, most teachers lack reliable tools to document students' value internalisation. Using a Research and Development design with the ADDIE framework, the tool was built on Krathwohl's taxonomy of the affective domain and supported by attitude theory, social cognitive theory, and the concepts of global citizenship and character education. Content validity was assessed using Aiken's V with five experts, followed by empirical testing with 182 participants in the pilot test and 498 participants in the field test. Item-total correlation and Cronbach's alpha were used to assess item performance and internal consistency, with reliability coefficients between 0.706 and 0.804. EFA revealed a general affective factor while retaining five theoretically relevant factors: receiving, responding, valuing, organisation, and characterisation. CFA proved that the measurement mod

title: A character education model based on deep learning in the teaching of Pancasila
abstract: This study developed and tested a Deep Learning-Based Character-Strengthening Education Model for Pancasila Education at the junior high school level in Bandar Lampung City, Indonesia. Using a mixed-methods design integrated with Research and Development (R&D), the study proceeded through six stages, from preliminary participatory observation and prototype development to expert and teacher validation, quasi-experimental testing, multilevel statistical analysis, and final model refinement. Participants comprised teachers and students from junior high schools across Bandar Lampung City, selected through random sampling. The results showed that understanding of Pancasila concepts increased by 25% in the experimental group, compared with 10% in the control group, with character-strengthening indicators – tolerance, integrity, responsibility and cooperation – also registering significantly greater gains (p

title: Traditional Lampung marriage from the perspective of local democracy: A study in the Megow Pak community
abstract: Marriage is both divine law and a socio-cultural mechanism for the Megow Pak Lampung community in passing down local values ​​between generations. This transition process is important to study as a crucial foundation for the realization of local democracy. This study aims to describe the traditional marriage mechanism of Megow Pak Lampung and its contribution to local democracy. This study uses a qualitative method with a narrative approach to explore and describe the results of the researcher's understanding as an academic in civic education and having experience with the traditional Megow Pak Lampung wedding. Data were obtained from participants through interviews, field notes, reflection journals, and literature. The research results show that Metagh and Sebambangan are voluntary marriage mechanisms, while Ramot and Nakad are the opposite. These various mechanisms open up space for deliberative democratic dialogue with cultural democracy in the practices of information transparency, respect for differing opinions, deliberation, equal social participation, the inheritance of democratic values, and respect for human dignity.

title: Beyond rationalism: Pancasila as a symbolic system
abstract: Pancasila has predominantly been interpreted within a rational-normative philosophical tradition that emphasises conceptual coherence, logical consistency, and systematic relationships among its five principles. While this approach has contributed significantly to the development of Pancasila philosophy, it remains limited in explaining how Pancasila functions as a living reality within Indonesian society. This study proposes an alternative interpretation by examining Pancasila through Ernst Cassirer’s philosophy of symbolic forms. Employing a qualitative philosophical approach, the research applies a conceptual adequacy test combined with interpretative conceptual analysis to evaluate the extent to which Pancasila fulfils the characteristics of a symbolic system. The analysis reconstructs five conceptual criteria derived from Cassirer’s theory—mediating function, meaning construction, collective dimension, experiential orientation, and independence from empirical verification—and systematically maps them onto the structure and functions of Pancasila. The findings demonstrate that each principle (sila) operates not merely as a normative proposition but as a symbolic form that media

title: Reconstructing civic identity in the digital age: Pancasila, collective memory, and the crisis of generation z's national imagination
abstract: In recent decades, globalisation has led to a decline in nationalism and a crisis of civic identity among Generation Z. This study aims to analyse the philosophical process underlying this phenomenon. This study uses an integrative review of Google Scholar and Garuda, along with theoretical frameworks including the theory of the nation-state, Benedict Anderson's The Imagined Community, and Maurice Halbwachs' Collective Memory. Previous studies have concluded that globalisation has led to a decline in nationalism among Generation Z and have linked this decline to failures in civic education. However, the philosophical process of how globalisation causes this crisis has not been explored. This study explores this philosophical process using a theoretical framework. The analysis concludes that nationalism and civic identity are products of national imagination, historical continuity, and the inheritance of collective memory about national identity. However, in the digital ecosystem, the dominance of global narratives interrupts this inheritance process and even creates a transnational imagination. title: Presentation-based media and information literacy: Grade 12 technical-vocational students’ lived experiences and perceived links to digital citizenship
abstract: This study explored how senior high school students experienced a researcher-developed 21st Century Skills Presentation Approach in Media and Information Literacy and what those experiences imply for educating responsible digital citizens. A descriptive phenomenological design was used with ten purposively selected Grade 12 technical-vocational students at a private Philippine school. Five participants were consistent honor students and five were lower-performing students; the categories broadened experiential variation rather than serving as comparison groups. Individual semi-structured interviews lasting 45-60 minutes were conducted online, transcribed verbatim, member-checked, and analyzed through horizonalization, meaning formulation, thematic clustering, and textural-structural synthesis. Five themes described the shared experience: a shift from passive participation toward motivated and responsible engagement; perceived growth in critical thinking, creativity, communication, and collaboration; difficulty adapting to learner-centered work, judging source credibility, coordinating groups, and managing time and technology; resilience through teacher and peer support, reflective

title: Piil Pesenggiri as a foundational framework for local wisdom-based education in promoting cultural identity and social cohesion within the SDGs perspective
abstract: This study examines Piil Pesenggiri as the basic framework of education based on local wisdom and its role in promoting cultural identity and social cohesion among the people of Lampung Pepadun. The study employed a descriptive qualitative approach, with a case study in Baradatu District, Way Kanan Regency. The research data were obtained through in-depth interviews with traditional leaders as well as document studies of the Kuntara Raja Niti customary law book and ethnopedagogical literature. The data were analysed thematically through the flow of reduction, presentation, and conclusion drawing, with validity tested through the triangulation of sources and techniques. The results of the study show that Piil Pesenggiri functions as a cultural norm of the Lampung Pepadun community, which animates four main values: Nemui Nyimah (friendliness), Nengah Nyappur (social involvement), Bejuluk Beadek (recognition of customary titles), and Sakai Sambayan (mutual cooperation). The consistency of this value in the oral traditions and the text of Kuntara Raja Niti confirms its position as an adaptive living law. Ethnopedagogically, the integration of Piil Pesenggiri in education effectively sh

title: The 2024 general election and the role of civic education in preventing social polarisation among youth
abstract: Indonesia’s 2024 general election unfolded amid intensifying global concerns about democratic resilience, algorithmic polarisation, and the erosion of deliberative public discourse. This study aims to analyse the role of Civic Education in preventing social polarisation among youth in the context of the 2024 Indonesian General Election, with specific attention to: (1) the dynamics of electoral polarisation, (2) factors contributing to youth vulnerability in the digital information landscape, and (3) the capacity of the Merdeka Curriculum to build democratic resilience among young citizens. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted across Scopus, Web of Science, and SINTA-indexed databases using keywords including “affective polarisation,” “digital political literacy,” “civic education,” “filter bubble,” and “democratic resilience,” yielding 36 articles meeting the inclusion criteria (peer-reviewed, 2017–2025, English and Indonesian). We applied policy analysis to Merdeka Curriculum documents for Pancasila and Civic Education. title: Internationalisation of Pancasila: Strengthening the character of the Indonesian diaspora against transnational ideologies
abstract: This study examines how transnational ideologies interact with Pancasila-based national identity among Indonesian citizens living in the Indonesia-Malaysia border region and in diaspora communities abroad. Drawing on digital questionnaires and in-depth interviews with Indonesian citizens, migrant workers, and diplomatic officials in Sabah (Malaysia), China, the United States, Canada, and Italy, the research identifies a significant development gap between North Kalimantan and Sabah that drives border communities' economic dependence on Malaysia, fuelling goods smuggling and irregular labour migration. Socially, the Indonesian diaspora in Sabah is found to be fragmented into ethnic-based communities, with migrant workers frequently facing discrimination, underscoring the importance of diplomatic protection in safeguarding their rights and sustaining harmonious Indonesia-Malaysia relations. The findings further show that transnational ideologies, particularly liberalism and radicalism, actively shape the political outlook of Indonesian citizens abroad, who can be categorised into three groups: those who uphold Pancasila, those inclined towards extreme liberalism, and those influenced

title: Counter hegemony against radicalism through local wisdom the sko tradition on the community Jambi Kerinci
abstract: This study examines the Kenduri Sko tradition of the Kerinci people in Jambi as a form of counter-hegemony against radical ideologies, drawing on an ethnographic qualitative approach conducted in Tarutung Village through in-depth interviews, participant observation, and documentation with traditional leaders, religious figures, and community members. Kenduri Sko, a ceremonial practice embodying cooperation, solidarity, tolerance, and spirituality, serves as a medium for transmitting cultural values across generations. Through collective participation, traditional leaders, religious figures, and community elders integrate messages of peace, deliberation, and anti-violence into ritual activities, reinforcing social cohesion and early detection of deviant behaviours. Analysis of the Tarutung Village Customary Book, particularly Law Nan 12, reveals codified norms opposing acts of extremism, reflecting the harmony of custom and religion as tools of resistance. The findings indicate that Kenduri Sko strengthens communal resilience, fosters critical awareness, and safeguards local identity against ideological infiltration. title: Constructing responsible citizenship: A social constructionist study of how teachers cultivate responsibility through pedagogical practices in Finland
abstract: This study examines how Finnish teachers construct values of responsible citizenship in their pedagogical practices. This qualitative case study involved six teachers from early childhood and primary education in Finland and usedsemi‑structured interviews. The data were analysed thematically, focusing on how teachers narrated responsibility in everyday routines, family–school partnerships, and references to civic institutions. The analysis identified seven interrelated strategies: encouraging self‑reliance, organising collective responsibility, promoting ethical awareness, assigning practical life tasks, facilitating work‑life orientation, modelling civic trust, and collaborating with families. These strategies show that responsibility is constructed through interaction, narrative, and institutional trust, as teachers integrate citizenship values in everyday routines, ethical framings, and examples drawn from Finland. Responsibility is thereby performed as both a personal practice and a civic virtue anchored in public institutions. The study advances global debates on citizenship education and social constructionism by illustrating how responsible citizenship is cultivated as a liv

title: Pancasila: The values of integrity and empathy in reconstructing the relationship between state officials and citizens in Indonesia
abstract: The article examines the rising incidence of corruption and apathetic behaviour among public officials in Indonesia, indicating a moral crisis in state governance. This condition reflects the weak implementation of Pancasila’s core values—particularly integrity and empathy—within bureaucratic practices and public leadership. The study aims to analyse the relevance of the values of integrity and empathy embedded in Pancasila's principles as a moral foundation for preventing corruption and for developing ethical public officials. This research uses a qualitative, descriptive-analytical approach, drawing on library research and content analysis of scholarly literature, official documents, and secondary data from credible sources. The analytical framework draws upon the theory of public integrity, empathic leadership, and ethical leadership theory. The findings indicate that the values of integrity and empathy in Pancasila serve a strategic function as catalysts for reconstructing the relationship between citizens and state administrators. title: Administrative service as civic practice: Pancasila-based public service ethics and the performance of educational support staff in a higher education faculty
abstract: Administrative and educational support staff (tenaga kependidikan) occupy a largely under-theorised position in the citizenship literature, even though they mediate the everyday relationship between higher education institutions and the students and citizens they serve. Drawing on the sociology of bureaucratic encounter and on Pancasila-based public service ethics, this study examines how the performance of faculty-level support staff at a public university in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, enacts – or fails to enact – civic values of hospitality, responsiveness and accountability in the delivery of everyday administrative services. Using a qualitative descriptive approach, the study analysed indicators of staff performance (work quality, task accuracy, initiative, and competence) alongside organisational, individual, and cultural factors that shape service delivery. The findings show that staff performance sustains a broadly courteous and orderly service culture, but is constrained by weak task awareness, uneven competence, inadequate systems and facilities, hierarchical bureaucratic culture, and insufficient reward and evaluation mechanisms. title: Civic nationalism as democratic mediation: Reinterpreting Indonesia’s civic education mandate through Deweyan progressivism
abstract: Civic education in Indonesia is mandated by Law No. 20 of 2003 to form both “democratic and responsible citizens” (Article 3) and citizens with “a sense of nationality and love of the homeland” (Elucidation of Article 37, paragraph 1). This article examines the normative coherence between these two mandates, arguing that civic education must not only build national identity but also cultivate citizens capable of reasoning, dialogue, participation, and responsibility within democratic life. Adopting a qualitative-philosophical approach that combines philosophical hermeneutics, ontological, epistemological, and axiological analysis, and immanent critique informed by John Dewey’s progressivism, the study identifies three loci of tension: a teleological tension between democratic citizenship and affective national orientation; an epistemic-pedagogical tension between inquiry, student agency, and value internalisation; and an axiological tension among democracy, human rights, pluralism, and nationality. title: The Collective memory as a based identity: Looking into religious bonding beyond nations
abstract: How does collective memory sustain bonds between societies separated by national borders? This study examines the relationship between Indonesia and Palestine through the lens of collective memory, with particular attention to its material, social, and mental dimensions. Using a qualitative case-study approach that combines historical inquiry, systematic literature review, and interviews with selected informants involved in solidarity practices for Palestine, the study explores how memory is formed, transmitted, and reproduced across time. The findings show that the material dimension is reflected in sacred architecture, scriptural references, and symbolic media that preserve Palestine in Indonesian Muslim memory. The social dimension is manifested in sermons, religious gatherings, fundraising initiatives, and solidarity movements that continually reproduce remembrance in collective life. The mental dimension appears in religiosity, empathy, and shared moral identification, through which Palestine is experienced not merely as a distant political issue but as a meaningful religious and humanitarian concern.
